title: Short Stuff: Christmas Lights
summary: Short Stuff holiday episode on the history of Christmas lights. Josh and Chuck trace how Edward H. Johnson, an Edison associate, lit the first electric Christmas tree in 1882 with 80 red, white and blue bulbs, then the rise of Christmas lights: early costs (a 16-bulb string at about $12 in 1890, roughly $375 today), the need for generators and electricians, GE's pre-assembled kits in 1903, prices falling by 1914, mainstream adoption by the 1930s, and the shift to white lights in the 1970s. They also cover color preferences, energy use statistics from 2011, and LED bulbs. Listener Daniel Montgomery suggested the topic.

segments.title: Opening and setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the pre-Christmas Short Stuff, credit listener Daniel Montgomery for the idea, and introduce the topic of Christmas lights.

segments.name: x
segments.title: Edward Johnson's first electric Christmas tree
segments.summary: Edward H. Johnson, a Edison associate and VP of the Edison Electric Light Company, hand-wired a Christmas tree with 80 red, white and blue lights shortly after the light bulb was invented. Live candles had been the previous norm. Reporter W. A. Crowfoot of the Detroit Post Tribune wrote about the display.

segments.title: Candles on Christmas trees
segments.summary: Background on Christmas tree candles, tied to Martin Luther and Prince Albert bringing the tradition to England, and the fire hazard of live candles.

segments.title: Early cost and spread of Christmas lights
segments.summary: Johnson's tree spurred others to light their trees. A 16-bulb string cost about $12 in 1890 (around $375 today), plus generators and electricians. A Library of Congress estimate put lighting a tree around 1903 at about $2,000. GE began selling pre-assembled kits in 1903, prices fell by 1914, and lights became mainstream in the 1930s.

segments.title: Mainstream adoption and competitions
segments.summary: Towns and government buildings lit their squares first, then homes by the 1930s. General Electric sponsored Christmas light competitions in the 1920s, and by the 1950s many streets were fully lit.

segments.title: White, colored and blue lights
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the switch to many white lights in the 1970s, personal tree preferences, and that Graceland was lit in blue. A Today's Homeowner 2023 survey found 16% of Americans prefer colored lights and 22% white.

segments.title: Energy use of Christmas lights
segments.summary: Christmas lights add to electricity use. A 2011 figure cites about $7.8 billion in spending and 6.63 billion extra kilowatt-hours, about 0.2% of U.S. electricity use. LEDs use much less power.

segments.title: Casey Wilson shout-out
segments.summary: Chuck praises comedian Casey Wilson, who has six Christmas trees, and recommends her book The Wreckage of My Presence.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Daniel Montgomery, wish listeners Merry Christmas, and mention an upcoming Christmas special. Show credits follow.
